findings.where: Screen 2 text and read ("The heat is held."); whatAmILookingAt ("With the heat locked", "The heat has a lock too"); screen 8 caption ("Move the piston or the heat")
findings.what: Each of these says the heat is held when the temperature is what is held, which goes against lesson 1's lesson that heat and temperature are different things, and it is wrong physics too, because heat flows out of a gas squeezed at a steady temperature; say "The temperature is held" to match the tag.

The brief promised that pressure is force over area, in pascals like stress, with the atmosphere about 10^5 Pa, but the lesson never says what pressure is or that 1 bar is 100 kPa, and lessons 4, 5 and 7 will need kPa (200 kPa × 0.001 m³, 10 m of seawater adds about 100 kPa, h = p ÷ ρg).

The brief's pV = mRT, with air's 287 J/(kg K), the 1 m³ receiver at 800 kPa absolute and 20 °C holding about 9.5 kg, and the 1.21 kg/m³ check, is missing, so the lesson never says that pV ÷ T measures the amount of gas, and screen 13's why then asserts "the amount of air follows the absolute pressure" without teaching it.

"A 10 V drop between two points still reads 10 V" is wrong for a meter that takes 100 V off every reading, because measured directly across the two points it would show −90 V; the offset only cancels when you read each point and subtract (440 and 430 show 340 and 330, still 10 apart).

findings.where: Practice, first paragraph (isolate, lock off, vent, "a gauge can stick")
findings.what: These safety steps and the stuck-gauge claim have no source in research.json or in the lesson's sources (the fact-check pass added them), so either cite public pressure-systems guidance such as HSE's or cut them down to what is sourced.

Each puzzle asks the exact example the SHOW screen before it just worked (1 bar gauge halved gives 3; floating from 300 K to 400 K gives 4 L at 2 bar; 500 L between 6 and 8 bar gauge gives 1,000 L; 20 to 40 °C is about 7%), so it tests reading, not understanding; change the numbers, for example 3 bar gauge halved gives 7 bar gauge.

The demonstration warms the gas from 27 °C to 127 °C, but the words work 20 °C to 40 °C, so the picture and the example don't match; either animate 20 to 40 °C or put the 300 K to 400 K numbers in the words.

The demonstration and the read-through still only show the box steady in absolute pressure and kelvin, so the red drift in gauge or °C, the contrast the screen is for, appears only if Dan taps the units; let the demonstration switch to gauge for its last second, or let the still show the drift.

"Pressure goes up with kelvin and down with volume. So ... pV ÷ T stays the same" skips a step, because going up with something is not the same as being in proportion to it; say "in proportion to kelvin, and in inverse proportion to volume".
The pressure law and Charles's law are both shown but never named, while Boyle's law is named; name them once, because he will meet them by name in his Level 3 course.
The brief's other receiver points are missing: at least 2 minutes between cut-in and cut-out, and that a higher pressure does not mean more flow; condensate appears only in the ignores list.

The blocks chart isn't drawn before Check and appears all at once afterwards, so the picture grows by about 130 px and the answer, Check and Why? buttons jump down; reserve its height (faint empty blocks) from the start.
The receiver is a blank rounded box over "compressor" with no label, so put "receiver" inside it, as screens 10 and 11 put "500 L".
Tie the answer back to the method screen 10 taught: at 9 bar its air would fill 4,500 L at 1 bar and at 7 bar 3,500 L, so 1,000 of 4,500 has gone, about 22%.
The caption sits at the card's left edge, outside the centred 30rem column that the lead, the steps and the buttons use; add .caption to the centred column.
"A cylinder of gas under a piston, a heater beneath it..." stays above the receiver screens, where no cylinder or heater is drawn.
It uses build jargon ("a receiver skin") and describes the piston's "three settings" and a heat "lock" as if Dan could switch them, when each screen sets them and no control does.
"The 3 L grows to 4 L" names a 3 L the explain has not introduced; say "3 L of gas at 2 bar absolute" first.
